question: A 68-year-old woman has chronic hyponatraemia: serum Na⁺ 116 mmol/L for >48 hours, with only mild drowsiness and no seizures. What is the maximum safe rate of sodium correction over the first 24 hours?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correcting by 20 mmol/L risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS), also called central pontine myelinolysis. The safe limit is ≤10–12 mmol/L/24 h in most patients.

Correct. For chronic hyponatraemia (>48 hours), the safe correction limit is ≤10–12 mmol/L in the first 24 hours, and ≤18 mmol/L in 48 hours. Exceeding this risks osmotic demyelination syndrome. In very high-risk patients (alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalaemia), the limit is ≤8 mmol/L/24 h.

This rate is far too rapid for chronic hyponatraemia and would cause osmotic demyelination syndrome. Rapid correction is only considered in acute severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma) with hypertonic saline — even then limited to 5 mmol/L bolus.

answers.text: No correction needed until sodium is below 110 mmol/L

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Symptoms drive urgency, not just the absolute level. This patient is drowsy at 116 mmol/L, which requires gradual correction. Waiting for 110 mmol/L risks missing the symptomatic threshold for intervention.

overallFeedback.feedback: The safe correction rate for chronic hyponatraemia is ≤10–12 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination syndrome. Only acute symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma) justifies rapid initial correction (1–2 mmol/L/h for up to 3–4 hours), still within the 24-hour limit.

Correct. ≤10–12 mmol/L/24 h is the safe ceiling for chronic hyponatraemia. Faster correction risks osmotic demyelination — an irreversible brainstem injury causing dysarthria, dysphagia, and locked-in syndrome.
